title: Arithmetic, Memory, and Jumps
summary: The unit covers immediate operands (Immediate Operand) and arithmetic instructions, the M extension (M-Erweiterung), bitwise logical instructions (Bitweise logische Befehle), and shifts. It then addresses byte addressing (Byteadressierung), word size (Wortbreite), alignment (Alignment), endianness, and 64-bit transfers between registers and main memory (Hauptspeicher). Finally, it examines unconditional and conditional jumps and branches (Sprünge und Branches) as mechanisms for controlling program flow.
keyFacts: `addi a, b, imm` adds the constant `imm` to the value in `b` and writes the result to `a`.
To subtract a constant, use `addi` with a negative constant; there is no separate `subi` instruction.
The immediate in `addi` is limited to 12 bits and is sign-extended when negative.
`addi a, x0, imm` copies a constant directly into the destination register because `x0` always contains zero.
`lui` loads a 20-bit portion into the upper bits; `addi` can add another portion.
Depending on the instruction, `mul`, `mulh`, `mulhsu`, and `mulhu` return the lower or upper product portion with different signedness interpretations.
`div` and `rem` operate on signed values; `divu` and `remu` operate on unsigned values.
`and`, `or`, and `xor` combine register values bit by bit.
Logical right shifts fill the leftmost positions with zeros; arithmetic right shifts preserve the sign bit.
Floating-point arithmetic is not part of the RISC-V base instruction set; `fadd` and `fsub` are examples of floating-point instructions.
Main memory usually consists of addressable bytes, each 8 bits; registers are a small number of fast temporary storage locations.
With an address width of $n$ bits, at most $2^n$ distinct byte addresses can be represented.
A 32-bit value occupies four consecutive byte addresses; a 64-bit value occupies eight.
A datum is aligned to an $n$-byte boundary when $A \bmod n=0$.
In little-endian order, the least significant byte is at the lowest address; in big-endian order, the most significant byte is.
In `ld a1, 8(s0)`, `a1` is the destination register, and the effective address is the value in `s0` plus 8.
In `sd a1, 8(s0)`, `a1` is the source, and its value is written to RAM starting at the effective address.
`beq`, `bne`, `blt`, and `bge` branch based on a comparison between two registers; an unconditional jump is always taken.

questions.prompt: In `addi a, b, imm`, what role does `imm` play?

options.text: A constant specified in the instruction

questions.explanation: `imm` is the immediate operand, a constant encoded directly in the instruction. `a` is the destination register and `b` is the source register.

questions.prompt: To subtract a constant in RISC-V, use `addi` with a negative constant; a separate `subi` instruction is not needed.
questions.explanation: Because it accepts negative immediate values, `addi` can also perform subtraction. The negative value is sign-extended.

questions.prompt: In `addi a, x0, imm`, ___ is copied into `a`.

options.text: the value of the program counter
the value of the next instruction

questions.explanation: Since `x0` always contains zero, the sum `0 + imm` is exactly the constant `imm`.

questions.prompt: How many bits wide is the immediate in `addi`?
questions.explanation: The immediate in `addi` is 12 bits wide. For larger constants, `lui` and `addi` can be combined, among other approaches.

questions.prompt: Which instructions require the M extension? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: `mulh`, `divu`, and `rem` are among the multiplication, division, and remainder instructions in the M extension. `and` and `addi` are not M-extension instructions.

questions.prompt: How do `and`, `or`, and `xor` work?

options.text: They compare only the most significant bits.
They shift the register values by one position.
They combine the source registers bit by bit.

questions.explanation: Each of these three instructions performs its respective logical operation separately at every bit position.

questions.prompt: Which right shift preserves the sign bit?
questions.explanation: In an arithmetic right shift (`sra`/`srai`), the sign bit is preserved. A logical right shift instead fills the leftmost positions with zeros.

questions.prompt: Floating-point arithmetic using instructions such as `fadd` and `fsub` is part of the RISC-V base instruction set.
questions.explanation: Floating-point arithmetic is not part of the base instruction set. `fadd` and `fsub` are floating-point instructions, but they require an extension.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes main memory in relation to registers?

options.text: Main memory is smaller than registers but faster.
Main memory contains only instructions, never data.
Main memory is just another name for secondary storage.
Main memory has greater capacity and holds data being processed.

questions.explanation: Registers are few in number and fast to access. RAM has greater capacity and holds the data being processed.

questions.prompt:
Which edge in the diagram represents the transfer from RAM to a register?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["RAM"] -->|Load| R["Register"]
    R -->|Store| M
    R --> C["Rechen- und Logikbefehle"]
    C --> R
```

options.text: The edge to the arithmetic unit
The return edge from the arithmetic unit

questions.explanation: `Load` loads data from RAM into a register. `Store` moves data in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: How many distinct byte addresses can be represented with an address width of 3 bits?
questions.explanation: With $n=3$, $2^n=2^3=8$. The addresses range from `000` to `111`.

questions.prompt: `b` contains the value 27. What value does `a` contain after `addi a, b, -9`?
questions.explanation: The negative constant is sign-extended and added: $27+(-9)=18$. The value 36 would result from incorrectly adding 9.

questions.prompt:
What output does this code produce, more precisely: what value does `t0` contain afterward?

```asm
lui  t0, 0x12345
addi t0, t0, 0x678
```
questions.explanation: `lui` first produces `0x12345000`. Adding `0x678` gives `0x12345678`.

questions.prompt: For the four bits, let `s1 = 1010` and `s2 = 1100`. What result does `xor s3, s1, s2` produce?
questions.explanation: XOR produces 1 exactly when the bits differ: `1010 XOR 1100 = 0110`. `1000` would be the result of AND, and `1110` the result of OR.

questions.prompt: What result does a logical right shift by one position produce for the 8-bit value `10110100`?
questions.explanation: With `srl`, one bit is removed on the right and a 0 is added on the left: `10110100` becomes `01011010`. `11011010` would result from an arithmetic right shift.

questions.prompt: Which mappings are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `mulhsu` returns the lower portion of the product.
`mulhu` returns the upper portion for two unsigned operands.
`mul` returns the lower portion of the product.

questions.explanation: `mul` returns the lower product portion, `mulhu` the upper portion for two unsigned operands, and `remu` the unsigned remainder. By contrast, `mulhsu` returns an upper product portion, and `divu` operates on unsigned values.

questions.prompt: Which of the following starting addresses is aligned for a 4-byte datum?
questions.explanation: Alignment to a 4-byte boundary means $A \bmod 4=0$. Only $12\bmod4=0$; the other addresses have a remainder of 2 or 3.

questions.prompt: The 32-bit value `0x6C2A91E7` begins at byte address `n`. Its bytes from most significant to least significant are `0x6C`, `0x2A`, `0x91`, `0xE7`. In little-endian order, the least significant byte is at `n`; the next more significant byte is at each subsequent address. Which byte is at `n+2`?
questions.explanation: In little-endian order, the bytes are stored starting at `n` as `0xE7`, `0x91`, `0x2A`, `0x6C`. Therefore, the byte at `n+2` is `0x2A`.

questions.prompt: `s0` contains 1000. What does `ld a1, 8(s0)` do?

options.text: It loads 64 bits from address 1008 into `a1`.
It loads 64 bits from address 992 into `a1`.
It loads 8 bits from address 1000 into `a1`.

questions.explanation: The effective address is $1000+8=1008$. `ld` loads a doubleword, or 64 bits, from RAM into the destination register `a1`.

questions.prompt: What role does `a1` play in `sd a1, 8(s0)`?

options.text: `a1` is the destination register for a load.
`a1` specifies the number of bits to shift.
`a1` is the source of the 64 bits to be stored.

questions.explanation: With `sd`, the first register is the source. The value from `a1` is written to RAM at address `Wert(s0)+8`.

questions.prompt:
What output does this code produce, more precisely: what value does `s0` contain at the end?

```asm
addi s3, x0, 4
addi s4, x0, 4
addi s0, x0, 1
bne  s3, s4, L1
addi s0, s0, 2
L1:
sub  s0, s0, s3
```
questions.explanation: `s3` and `s4` are equal, so the code does not branch to `L1`. Then $s0=1+2-4=-1$.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does `bge r1, r2, ziel` branch?

options.text: When `r1` is greater than or equal to `r2`

questions.explanation: `bge` stands for “branch if greater or equal.” The branch is taken if the first register value is greater than or equal to the second.

questions.prompt: Which statements about immediate constants are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Subtraction by a constant can be expressed using `addi` with a negative immediate.
`addi a, x0, imm` can write a constant directly to `a`.
The immediate in `addi` is limited to 12 bits.
A negative immediate value is processed without sign extension.
`lui` alone always automatically adds all lower bits of an arbitrarily large constant.

questions.explanation: `addi` can subtract using negative constants, but it has only a 12-bit immediate and uses sign extension. Using `x0`, a constant can be written directly to a register; `lui` alone does not add lower bits.

questions.prompt: Which instruction returns the upper portion of the product when the first operand is interpreted as signed and the second as unsigned?
questions.explanation: `mulhsu` returns the upper product portion with a signed first operand and an unsigned second operand. By contrast, `mulh` uses two signed operands.

questions.prompt: An `AND` mask leaves a 1 at a bit position only when both operands contain a 1 there.
questions.explanation: For AND, $1\text{ AND }1=1$; all other input combinations produce 0. Therefore, only the shared 1-bits remain.

questions.prompt: Which combination correctly describes the two right shifts of the value `10110100` by one position?
questions.explanation: `srl` adds a 0 on the left and produces `01011010`. `sra` copies the leading 1-bit and produces `11011010`.

questions.prompt:
Which label belongs on the edge from RAM to the register?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["RAM"] -->|?| R["Register"]
    R --> C["Rechen- und Logikbefehle"]
    C --> R
```
questions.explanation: A load transfers data from RAM to a register. A store would denote the opposite direction, from the register to RAM.

questions.prompt: Which statements about memory cells and word size are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A 32-bit instruction must always be read in four separate byte accesses.
A typical addressable memory cell contains 8 bits, or one byte.
A byte address identifies only the location of a complete 32-bit value.
A 32-bit value occupies four consecutive byte addresses.
The processor's word size and the size of an addressable memory cell are different properties.

questions.explanation: Memory is usually byte-addressable, so a 32-bit value occupies four bytes. The processor's word size is not the same as the size of an individual memory cell; a single access does not necessarily have to be byte-wide.

questions.prompt: `s0` contains 1000. Which byte addresses are written by `sd a1, 8(s0)`?
questions.explanation: The effective address is $1000+8=1008$. A 64-bit store occupies eight bytes, so it uses addresses 1008 through 1015 inclusive.

questions.prompt: Little-endian order is technically necessary because this byte order became universally established through Intel.
questions.explanation: Intel's prevalence explains the widespread use of little-endian order, but it is not a technical necessity. Big-endian order is also possible.

questions.prompt: For this question, a 4-byte datum at address $A$ is aligned if $A \bmod 4 = 0$. x86 can allow unaligned accesses; some ARM types have stricter alignment requirements. A 4-byte access begins at byte address 6. Which statement is correct?

options.text: All x86 processors must reject the access, and all ARM processors must allow it.
An x86 processor that allows unaligned accesses may permit the access; for some ARM types, it may violate the stricter alignment requirement.
Address 6 is aligned because it is divisible by 2.
Alignment matters only for jump instructions, not for data accesses.

questions.explanation: $6 \bmod 4 = 2$, so the address is unaligned for a 4-byte datum. According to the properties stated in the question, an x86 processor can allow unaligned accesses; for some ARM types, the address may violate the stricter requirement.

questions.prompt:
In this RISC-V code, `x0 = 0`. `addi rd, rs, n` writes `rs + n` to `rd`; `add` adds two registers, and `sub` subtracts the second register from the first. `bne r1, r2, L` branches to `L` if the register values differ. A jump to a label resumes execution there; instructions before the label are skipped, and instructions starting at the label are executed.

What value does `s0` contain after the code executes?

```asm
addi s3, x0, 4
addi s4, x0, 7
addi s0, x0, 20
addi s1, x0, 6
bne  s3, s4, L1
add  s0, s0, s1
L1:
sub  s0, s0, s3
```
questions.explanation: `s3` and `s4` contain 4 and 7. Because they differ, `bne` branches to `L1` and skips the addition. The subtraction at the label is executed: `s0 = 20 − 4 = 16`.

questions.prompt: For `ld a1, 8(s0)`, effective address = ___.
questions.explanation: The offset is added to the value in the base register. The destination register `a1` does not affect the address calculation.

questions.prompt: The 5-bit pattern `11110` represents −2 in two's-complement notation. Which combination uses this meaning correctly for addition with a constant?

options.text: The value is +2; use `addi a, b, 2`.
The value is +30; use `subi a, b, 2`.
The value is −1; use `addi a, b, 1`.
The value is −2; use `addi a, b, -2`.

questions.explanation: With five bits, `11110` corresponds to the signed value −2. In RISC-V, subtraction by a negative constant is expressed using `addi` and sign extension.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the relationship between the ISA and RISC-V load/store instructions? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Disassembly automatically turns a store into an arithmetic instruction.
A load transfers data from RAM to a register, and a store transfers it in the opposite direction.
In RISC-V, registers are only names for memory addresses in RAM.
RISC-V arithmetic instructions generally use operands directly from RAM.
The ISA specifies the observable effects of register, load, and store instructions.

questions.explanation: The ISA specifies instructions, registers, and their observable effects. RISC-V follows a load/store architecture: arithmetic instructions operate on registers, while load and store instructions handle data transfers.

questions.prompt: A 64-bit value is stored in ordinary 8-bit memory cells. How many consecutive byte addresses does it require?
questions.explanation: 64 bits divided by 8 bits per byte equals 8 bytes. Therefore, a 64-bit word size does not describe the size of an individual memory cell.

questions.prompt:
What output does this code produce, more precisely: what value does `s0` contain at the end?

```asm
addi s1, x0, 10
addi s2, x0, 12
xor  s3, s1, s2
addi s0, x0, 1
bne  s3, s2, L1
addi s0, s0, 4
L1:
add  s0, s0, s3
```
questions.explanation: `10` is `1010` and `12` is `1100`; their XOR is `0110`, or 6. Since 6 is not equal to 12, the code branches to `L1`, skips the addition of 4, and ends with $1+6=7$.

questions.prompt: The 32-bit value `0x5C7E91A3` begins at byte address 128. Its bytes from most significant to least significant are `0x5C`, `0x7E`, `0x91`, `0xA3`. In little-endian order, the least significant byte is at the lowest address; the next more significant byte is at each subsequent address. A 4-byte datum at address $A$ is aligned if $A \bmod 4 = 0$. Which statements are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The most significant byte 0x5C is at address 131.
Address 128 is aligned for a 4-byte datum.

questions.explanation: In little-endian order, the bytes are at addresses 128 through 131 in the order `0xA3`, `0x91`, `0x7E`, `0x5C`. Thus c and e are correct. Also, 128 is divisible by 4, so a is correct as well.

questions.prompt: Which instructions return the upper portion of a 32-bit-by-32-bit product? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `mulhsu` for one signed and one unsigned operand

questions.explanation: The three upper-product variants are `mulh`, `mulhsu`, and `mulhu`; they differ in how they interpret signedness. `mul` returns the lower product portion, and `rem` returns a remainder.

questions.prompt:
What output does this code produce, more precisely: what value does `s2` contain at the end?

```asm
addi s0, x0, 5
addi s1, x0, 8
blt  s0, s1, L1
addi s2, x0, 0
j    Ende
L1:
addi s2, x0, 1
Ende:
add  s2, s2, s0
```
questions.explanation: Since $5<8$, `blt` branches to `L1` and sets `s2` to 1. The code then adds `s0=5`, giving 6.

questions.prompt:
Which description matches the possible data flow in the diagram?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["RAM"] -->|Load| R["Register"]
    R --> C["Rechen- und Logikbefehle"]
    C --> R
    R -->|Store| M
```

options.text: A store loads data from RAM into a register
Load registers from RAM only and never write them back
Load data from RAM, process it in a register, and store the result back in RAM
Modify RAM directly with an arithmetic instruction, without using registers

questions.explanation: The data flow is a load from RAM into a register, processing with register operands, and then a store back to RAM. This is the load/store architecture.

questions.prompt: A value such as `0x12345678` does not fit entirely in a 12-bit immediate. Which strategy matches the RISC-V syntax described?

options.text: Load the upper portion with `lui` and add another portion with `addi`
Shift the value into main memory with `srl`
Fetch the value from RAM with `beq` and add to it with `j`
Automatically generate an arbitrarily large constant with `and` and `xor`

questions.explanation: `lui` loads a 20-bit portion into the upper bits; `addi` adds the lower portion. The other instructions are not used to construct a large constant.

questions.prompt: Given `s0 = 1000` and the instructions `ld a1, 8(s0)` and `sd a1, 8(s0)`, which statements are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: For `ld`, `a1` is the source; for `sd`, it is the destination.
The transfer uses only byte addresses 1000 through 1007.
`sd` writes the value in `a1` to RAM.
The 64-bit transfer uses byte addresses 1008 through 1015.

questions.explanation: The offset 8 gives address 1008, and 64 bits occupy eight bytes there, through address 1015. `ld` loads into `a1`, while `sd` writes the value in `a1` to memory.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly compare conditional branches? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `bne` always branches, regardless of the register values.
Other ISAs such as x86 can check status flags from a previous arithmetic operation.
A conditional branch is taken only when its condition is met.
`bne r1, r2, ziel` directly checks whether the registers differ.
Every conditional branch must first evaluate a status register.

questions.explanation: In RISC-V, `bne` compares the two registers directly and branches only if they are unequal. Other ISAs may instead use status flags from a previous arithmetic operation; a branch is never taken unconditionally when its condition is not met.

levels.title: Practice: Bits, Bytes, and Jumps in Everyday Life

questions.prompt: You are developing a navigation app: at each intersection, it checks whether the requested street is closed. If it is closed, the program chooses an alternative; otherwise, it follows the route. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The app checks a condition and then decides which part of the program to execute. Conditional branches such as `beq` or `bne` serve exactly this purpose.

questions.prompt: In which situations are bitwise logic and bit masks especially useful?

options.text: A network protocol checks several independent flags in a header.
A smartphone stores several on/off switches compactly in a bit mask.
Image processing uses a mask to isolate a color channel in packed pixel data.

questions.explanation: AND, OR, and XOR operate on individual bits, so they are suitable for compact flags and masks, for example in status fields or packed pixel data. Alphabetically sorting names, by contrast, is not a bitwise operation.

questions.prompt: How many different bit patterns can a 12-bit field contain?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bit positions can be 0 or 1. Therefore, there are $2^{12}=4096$ different bit patterns.

questions.prompt: You are reading a 32-bit number from four bytes stored by another system. Is this statement correct: without knowing the byte order, the numeric value generally cannot be reconstructed reliably?
questions.explanation: In little-endian and big-endian formats, the bytes of a multi-byte value are stored in different orders in memory. The software must know which endianness is used to assemble the numeric value correctly.

questions.prompt: In a data structure, the ABI in use requires a 64-bit timestamp to begin at an 8-byte boundary. Why might the compiler insert extra bytes before the timestamp?

options.text: To make the timestamp begin at an 8-byte boundary
To automatically reorder the bytes into little-endian order
To convert a floating-point number into an integer
To turn the timestamp into a conditional branch

questions.explanation: Padding can align an address to the 8-byte boundary required by the ABI. This alignment can make accesses to multi-byte values easier or faster.

questions.prompt: A microcontroller uses 16-bit addresses for individual bytes. How many distinct byte addresses can it represent?
questions.explanation: With $n$ address bits, $2^n$ distinct byte addresses are possible. For 16 bits, that is $2^{16}=65536$ addresses.

questions.prompt: In a game, 64-bit coordinates are loaded from RAM, processed in registers, and then written back. Which architectural principle does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: In a load/store architecture, load instructions bring data into registers, arithmetic instructions operate on it there, and store instructions write results back to main memory.

questions.prompt: You store a 64-bit value in byte-addressable RAM. How many consecutive bytes does it occupy?
questions.explanation: A byte contains 8 bits. Therefore, a 64-bit value requires $64/8=8$ consecutive bytes.

questions.prompt: A compiler translates `points -= 3` without loading the number 3 separately from memory. Which idea does it typically use?

options.text: `mulh` with the upper half of the product

questions.explanation: RISC-V has no separate `subi` instruction; subtraction can be expressed as addition of a negative immediate. The negative 12-bit immediate is extended to the register width by sign extension.

questions.prompt: You are analyzing large counter readings in a measurement system: two signed 32-bit values are multiplied, and the result may require more than 32 bits. Which RISC-V support is relevant?

options.text: `mul` returns the lower portion and `mulh` the upper portion of the signed product
`fsub` stores the value in main memory

questions.explanation: The M extension provides separate instructions for the lower and upper portions of a product. For signed 32-bit operands, `mul` returns the lower portion and `mulh` the upper portion of the 64-bit product.
